joint_render.prompt:
A single full-bleed colour PHOTOGRAPHIC CONTACT SHEET of three new, carefully composed documentary photographs for an English gardening book; they will be cut apart. Canvas aspect 1.47 wide to 1 high. Precise panel layout: a vertical seam at 45.5% of the canvas width. LEFT COLUMN contains two equal-height 4:3 landscape photos, split at exactly half the canvas height. RIGHT COLUMN is one unbroken 4:5 portrait photograph the whole height. Hard straight seams, zero gaps and borders; no captions, letters, numbers, arrows or drawn lines anywhere. Real unstaged documentary photographs, not painting, stylised illustration or diagram. Reference 4 is an existing printed page to read only for the three actions and ordering; never imitate its drawings, type or layout. Real camera refs 1–3 show John, his working clothes and the textures of his Cornish home garden.

Make all three in one go, same spring afternoon with gentle overcast side light, same real loamy earth and short, dense, subtly uneven lawn. On the left a close ground-level working view of John's small lawn near the weathered pale horizontal timber fence on its low grey-buff wall. Allow working hands, sleeves and part of John's body in frame. Keep real scale consistent between the two left frames: never shrink the gardener or invent giant artificial blocks of turf. Same checked overshirt over a dark T-shirt, jeans, brown work shoes. A crop below the face is absolutely fine when the action is the subject. Skin, fabric, grass and soil with photographic detail. Restrained natural colours and little distracting background. Give every photo its own clean edge within the sheet.

TOP LEFT photo = LIFT. The turf is still right way up. A few straight spade cuts divide a small patch of tightly mown live lawn into rectangles approx 22 by 40 cm. John is using a normal flat, square-ended steel spade, its single straight wood shaft held LOW and diagonal, blade sliding HORIZONTALLY just BELOW the mat of roots along the soil surface. Clearly visible rectangular steel blade between ground and sod, going under and just raising one end of a single shallow rectangle of grass at the near edge. Side view in three-quarters, enough to see the green short grass upper face and a ragged root-bound brown underside only 3–5cm thick. Adjacent previously lifted space shows flat, shallow exposed soil level. Hands, boot and handle anatomically credible. No deep hole, no turning a tall chunk of earth; the close photo is chiefly the material and tool. The short grass must look like lawn grass growing from roots, not a manufactured carpet. Keep the entire blade/lift contact centrally in this panel.

BOTTOM LEFT photo = STACK. The same John in the same clothes folds back a front corner of an opaque dark bottle-green tarp to show a small squat pile of cut turves beside the new bed. Real manageable freshly cut slabs casually laid in 4–5 irregular courses in a broad stable stack under knee height, horizontal root-bound soil slabs with slightly offset ends and crumbly edges. EVERY turf is UPSIDE DOWN, damp brown soil and fine roots UPPERMOST, sparse crushed short grass blades tucked at the UNDERSIDE of each sod. The visible top of the stack is BROWN earth. Occasional dull green blades caught between courses make the orientation legible, but avoid neon green stripes, long hanging hay, or alternating grass-up and down. Tarp covers rear/top of the stack, casually folded back just enough to reveal top and layers on the near side; one or two bricks or stones still weigh down the far edge and hem. Johns working hand touching the cover gives scale. Subject fills this photo; not a pallet or manufactured loam bricks.

RIGHT, FULL-HEIGHT portrait photo = a real trench side, fresh burial as a separate use for the same turves. Camera is LOW INSIDE an actual narrow open double-digging trench looking almost straight at a freshly exposed SOIL FACE, nearly filling the frame. This must look convincingly like standing at an excavation looking at its backfilled end. The face is embedded in the ground, crosses the frame side-to-side, irregular edge and subtle receding return of the trench at one side, small amount of loose soil at its foot. No freestanding soil cube, no glass, no roots arranged for display, no illustration or drawn diagram. Top of frame catches a SMALL strip of loose brown topsoil at the freshly worked surface; no green lawn growing on top of this cultivated bed. The top half of the face is dark crumbly garden TOPSOIL backfilled from the adjacent trench with ordinary aggregates, little pebbles and fine roots; naturally rough spade marks. At approximately HALFWAY DOWN the portrait photo (about 48–52% height, including at its RIGHT edge where an outside label will point later), expose just the edge of a freshly buried shallow slab of INVERTED TURF. Its soil-root backing on top and a thin ragged irregular seam of crushed dull olive-green, yellowed and straw-coloured short grass blades POINTING DOWN into the loosened earth. The grass is still readable as blades even at small printed size, embedded and flattened. The seam continues right across the rightmost fifth of the photo. It must not read as a lawn growing horizontally in mid-air, a bright unbroken green stripe, a timber board or an empty cavity. BELOW this seam (lower 45% of frame) lighter warm brown loosened SUBSOIL, earthy angular clods of varying sizes resting against each other, fractures and small shadowed crevices left by the fork. No boulders. Set fine highlights on the freshly exposed natural soil and give the buried grass edge just enough contrast to be visible. In this right photo, no gardener, shovel, props or annotations. No staging of piles. All three photographs sharply readable at book size.
references: Page 162 of the source section, rendered for visual reference
joint_render.wardrobe: Checked shirt, jeans and brown shoes as in real H08 / J01. One working session, two alternative uses of fresh turf.

approval.scope: Page 162 photographic proof and all three images
